extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of poetry; literary critics and anyone learning practical criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reading, interpreting, and judging poems in classroom or critical practice, with a catalogue of common reading-difficulties and concrete evaluative dimensions used in protocol responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary aim of criticism: improvement in communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The one and only goal of all critical endeavours ... is improvement in communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical rules and principles are means to attain finer, more precise, more discriminating communication. Emphasises demonstrating value by communicating what is valuable rather than merely asserting valuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles as aids not substitutes for discernment
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical principles ... can never be a substitute for discernment though they may assist us to avoid unnecessary blunders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warnings that even the best critical formulas can be misapplied; they help wise critics but mislead fools. Beware crude application; remember subtle senses and apply principles finely rather than mechanically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to get the relevant mental condition/experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Our prime endeavour must be to get the relevant mental condition and then see what happens. Without the capacity to get the experience critical principles cannot help us at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before judgment, critic should aim to re-create the mental/experiential state pertinent to the poem; valuation follows from adequately achieving that state.

rubrics_metrics.name: A. Make out the plain (prose) sense of the poem
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulty of making out the plain sense of poetry — its prose sense, its plain overt meaning, as a set of ordinary, intelligible English sentences, and its feeling, tone, and intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many readers—even good ones—fail to construe the literal sense; failure affects subsequent judgment. Treat prose-sense and intended tone as primary diagnostic tasks (analogy: construe as a schoolboy would construe Caesar).

rubrics_metrics.name: B. Sensuous apprehension (form, movement, rhythm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words in sequence have a form to the mind's ear and tongue; they have a movement and may have a rhythm. Readers differ in capacity to perceive this sensuous form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish critics who immediately perceive rhythm/form from those who must build it laboriously; this affects appreciation of verse qualities and must be accounted for in evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: C. Role and variability of imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulties connected with the place of imagery (principally visual) in poetic reading; readers differ immensely in capacity to visualise and in the importance they attach to imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Images are erratic: vivid images evoked in one mind may differ from those in another and may not match the poet's images. Critics should avoid overvaluing poetry solely on subjective imagery and note these divergences.

rubrics_metrics.name: D. Mnemonic irrelevances (personal associations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Powerful influence of mnemonic irrelevances — the reader's being reminded of personal scenes, erratic associations, or emotional reverberations from unrelated past events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such intrusions mislead judgment; relevance is hard to define but some instances are easy to diagnose. Critics should watch for personal associations colouring responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: E. Stock responses (pre-formed reader reactions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical traps from stock responses when poem seems to involve views/emotions already prepared in the reader, so the reader's response may play a larger role than the poem's provocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be on guard for redistribution of credit between poet and reader; stock responses can cause injustice by attributing the reader's preconceptions to the poem (or vice versa).

rubrics_metrics.name: F. Sentimentality (excessive response)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentimentality is a peril — an over-facility in certain emotional directions; it concerns the due measure of response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for over-easy emotional reactions that exaggerate a poem's merits; distinguish natural emotional appeal from sentimental excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: G. Inhibition / Hardness of heart (under-response)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inhibition is a positive phenomenon (sometimes called Hardness of Heart) and affects the measure of response as much as sentimentality does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics must account for readers whose affective restraint leads to under-appreciation; neither over-response nor under-response should be mistaken for the poem's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: H. Doctrinal adhesions (reader's beliefs affecting judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrinal adhesions: poetry may seem to contain or imply views and beliefs about the world; the reader's convictions may then influence estimate of the poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question what bearing the truth-value of implicated beliefs has on poetic worth; distinguish genuinely contained beliefs from misread implications and avoid letting unrelated convictions dominate evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: I. Technical presuppositions (mistaking means for ends)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects of technical presuppositions: when something is once well done in a fashion we expect it thereafter; technique that failed once gets discredited for all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid judging poetry from outside by technical details (means) instead of their effects (ends). Be cautious attributing success/failure solely to technique; don't 'judge pianists by their hair.'

rubrics_metrics.name: J. General critical preconceptions (theoretical prior demands)
rubrics_metrics.description: General critical preconceptions — prior demands made upon poetry due to theories (conscious or unconscious) about its nature and value — intervene between reader and poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These preconceptions can prevent the reader from receiving what the poem offers; critics should be aware of and, where possible, bracket theoretical biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluative dimensions: thought, feeling, metre, expression (table)
rubrics_metrics.description: A suggested scheme for evaluating passages along axes: Thought, Feeling, Metre, and Expression with subcategories: True/False; Remarkable/Commonplace; Profound/Obvious; Original/Trite; Vivid/Confused/Dull/Convincing/Obscure/Tame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these paired descriptors (as exemplified in the page's table) to classify responses and disagreements; they provide concrete vocabulary for distinguishing kinds of praise and blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of form to theme (metre and expression fit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the chosen form (metre, diction, line-length) suits the poem's thought and theme — e.g., whether rugged metre makes the best setting, or whether verse is merely prose chopped to fit metre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in protocols: metre carrying emotional speech, metre lending dignity, or metre and necessary accents being awkward. Judge fit of form to content rather than form in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and condensation of language
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate choice of words: concise everyday language vs ornate/verbal embroidery; condensation where each word bears multiple meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protocols praise 'topping condensation' and avoidance of vapid adjectives; criticize prose-like diction or rhetorical platitudes. Consider whether diction drives home the thought or dilutes it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative/contextual referencing (use of analogies and other poets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers often compare passages to other poets/works (e.g., Wordsworth, Browning, Shakespeare) as part of evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons can illuminate affinities or expose derivative traits, but may also reflect mnemonic irrelevances or technical presuppositions; use comparative references judiciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of multiple readings (progressive revelation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsequent readings can reveal subtleties, clarify rhythm, and deepen appreciation; first impressions may change on rereading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage repeated readings to perceive cadence, hidden subtlety, and changing responses; protocols note that some passages 'wear better' with concentrated successive readings.
